projectTitle: CLiPPR - Chloroplast Library for inducible PPRs
tagline: Making the chloroplast switchable: inducible designer PPR proteins paired with synthetic 5'UTRs
summary: Chloroplasts are arguably the cheapest protein factories available (around 90% of global primary production, up to 70% of a plant cell's protein as transgenic product, linear rather than capital-intensive scaling), but they lack the one tool microbial hosts have: inducibility, so growth and production compete permanently and a toxic product means no plant at all. CLiPPR outsources that inducibility to the nucleus: nuclear-encoded, inducibly expressed synthetic pentatricopeptide repeat proteins are imported into the plastid, where they bind matched synthetic 5'UTRs placed upstream of a chloroplast gene and switch translation up or down by three mechanisms (blocking the start codon, protecting an unstable 5'UTR from exonucleases, or resolving a hairpin over the ribosome binding site). The team designed 30 fully synthetic 5'UTRs de novo, produced, purified and tested 19 new-to-nature PPR proteins, reported the highest transgene expression yet recorded in a chloroplast in vitro, and validated across three systems of rising complexity: chloroplast cell-free extract, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, and Nicotiana benthamiana. It won Best Alternative Platform and was nominated for Part Collection, Education, Presentation, Wiki and Foundational Advance.

dry.frameworks: The computational work is sequence and assembly engineering rather than structure prediction, and it is tightly coupled to a hard constraint: PPRs are long tandem repeats, and the high GC content of the C. reinhardtii nuclear genome makes conventional gene synthesis of those repetitive stretches expensive or impossible, which is what forced an organism-specific toolbox instead of ordering full coding sequences. Adapting the published GRASP Golden Gate toolbox (Dennis et al. 2025, consensus S-type repeats with a programmable PPR code, 42 level-1 modules assembling 9-, 14- and 19-nt binders) from E. coli to Chlamydomonas meant codon-optimising every module, which shifts the Golden Gate fusion sites and therefore changes assembly fidelity and module boundaries, a set of interdependent decisions the team first worked through by hand. They placed the new fusion sites inside the ARELF motif (the most variable codons in the repeat, giving the largest overhang pool), pulled C. reinhardtii codon usage from the Kazusa table, excluded every codon below 50% relative abundance among the most abundantly expressed proteins, searched the remaining ARELF translations for overhang sets, and scored candidates with the NEB ligase fidelity calculator against a target above 75%, first running the original GRASP level 0 and level 1 overhangs through the same calculator to get a baseline on the same scale rather than comparing a prediction against a published measurement. B- and D-modules were intronized per Baier et al., offered with and without the LHCBM1i2 intron. Binding was validated biophysically by fluorescence polarisation to extract dissociation constants, with one optimised PPR reaching a Kd among the best in the literature.
dry.dataviz: The wiki is unusually honest and unusually readable. Every page carries a per-page inventory in the subtitle ('7 sections / 17 pictures / 10 references'), a key-achievements list before any narrative, and a scroll progress indicator themed as a PPR walking along its binding sites ('PPR Bound Site 1 / 8'), with a Reinhardt mascot reacting to the content. Negative results are given the same prominence as positive ones: the XRN-1 titration and pair screening are reported as showing the nuclease is barely active under the chosen conditions, with the reason stated (room temperature and a buffer chosen to keep the chloroplast extract working rather than to keep the nuclease happy), followed by the redesigned assay that removed the extract and the translation step entirely; the semi-automated purification is reported as robust and reproducible but too low-yielding, with a recommendation about which other teams it would still suit. The Chlamydomonas screen reports that only a handful of mNeonGreen-positive transformants were usable because of their transplastomic background. The software is published as form-driven Colab notebooks with a 'click to explore our tools' interface, and the codon-usage comparison is given as a full 64-codon table with per-codon percentage-point differences between C. reinhardtii and E. coli rather than a summary statistic.
dry.datascience: The characterisation campaign is a throughput argument. Building and testing a library of this size by hand was not feasible, so three automation technologies were made integral to the experimental design rather than bolted on. An Echo 525 acoustic liquid handler, programmed with the PyEcho script, assembled all large assays (the largest replacing 868 final pipetting steps per replicate) and, by dispensing 25 nl droplets, allowed reaction volumes to be cut to a quarter of the 10 ul manual minimum, which both saved purified PPR protein and removed the pipetting inaccuracy inherent in sub-0.5 ul manual additions; planning the plate layout in software also made reagent demand calculable in advance (including when to buy expensive XRN-1), made pipetting-scheme errors catchable before they happened, and cut run-to-run variance because a 384-well plate is assembled in under five minutes rather than over an hour of reagents sitting out of the freezer. The BMG Clariostar autoinjector dispensed furimazine for the NanoLuc reporter at an identical incubation time every run, measurably lowering standard deviation against manual addition. A 96-well semi-automated protein purification workflow adapted from the Baker Lab protocol combined IMAC and automated size-exclusion chromatography so purification and characterisation happened in one run.
dry.software: PPR-opt, released as two form-driven Google Colab notebooks that run entirely remotely with no local install: PPR-opt Designer builds a PPR for a single target RNA sequence in a chosen host organism, and PPR-opt Inventory generates a whole GRASP-style toolbox able to clone every possible PPR for that organism. It automates the process the team first did manually: codon-optimising each PPR module for the target organism and redistributing the Golden Gate module boundaries accordingly. The team states plainly that all outputs are software predictions not yet experimentally validated, and that so far one PPR from the resulting Chlamy-GRASP toolbox has been successfully transformed into the C. reinhardtii nucleus. Alongside it they published the first PPR parts collection in the iGEM Registry: matched sets of synthetic 5'UTRs and their corresponding PPR proteins with sequence information, functional descriptions and characterisation data, plus the Chlamy-GRASP level 0 and level 1 modules; the wiki repository is gitlab.igem.org/2026/marburg.

good.publicEngagement: Marburg's education work is explicitly meta: they did not just build activities, they studied how to build them, after their first Girls' Day event prompted the question of what happens once an event is over. They reviewed the literature, consulted 15 experts across education, science communication and evaluation research, and found that existing iGEM documentation covers how outreach was organised but almost never how to ground it in theory or evaluate it beyond whether participants enjoyed it. Four outputs followed. A curriculum-aligned Teaching Toolbox ('Die CLiPPR Toolbox'), co-designed with education experts and aligned to the four German KMK national competency domains, tested with seven teachers at three schools and revised on their feedback. Plasmid Panic, an escape game playable by anyone over 12 with no scientific background, distributed through schools and with iGEM Patras in English and German. A SciComm and Evaluation Guide written specifically for future iGEM teams, covering how to set goals, pick evaluation methods and feed findings back. And a documented Evidence and Feedback process, published so others can see not only what was made but why, what changed and what was learned. Three expert quotations frame the whole approach: 'Reach is not impact, and satisfaction is not learning' (Dorothee Menhart), and 'Why are we communicating, and why should people care?' (Dr. Sascha Vogel).
good.ihp: 45 stakeholders, organised by the six application domains the technology touches (scientific impact, agriculture, space, molecular farming, environment and sustainability, law and regulations) rather than by job title, and the design changes are specific and attributed. Dr. Silvia Ramundo rejected the team's original plan to base the 'resolving' 5'UTR on Prikyl et al., where the hairpin the PPR resolves also contains the ribosome binding site, and recommended a design in which the PPR site and the RBS are locally disconnected so the PPR cannot interfere with ribosome binding; the team adapted to the Rojas et al. 2019 binding mechanism as a result. Prof. Ralph Bock (Max Planck Institute of Molecular Plant Physiology, a pioneer of chloroplast transformation) strongly advised dropping variable RBS testing and sticking to his validated Shine-Dalgarno sequence for predictable chloroplast translation, which they did. Prof. Alison Smith's input led them to combine two well-established repressible parts, the MetE and THI4 promoters, in one construct specifically to minimise leakiness, after Dr. Reimo Zoschke identified leakiness as the real unsolved problem ('what remains problematic are tight systems'). Tania Ryzhkova and another adviser steered characterisation away from an EMSA toward a fluorescence polarisation assay and then advised on RNase-free practice, labelled-RNA design, protein concentration ranges and controls, and on the analysis. An interview with an explosives-degradation expert made them realise phytoremediation bottlenecks come from pollutant kinetics and bioavailability rather than chloroplast gene timing, so they dropped that application. Prof. Yuri Gleba supplied the economic case (recombinant protein from plants at around 100 USD per kilogram; plants scale linearly while fermentation requires buying the next-size bioreactor), and Elena Lesch and Farley Kwok advised on testing in the 2021 Marburg chloroplast cell-free extracts rather than only E. coli, warning that such extracts are far less common than standard E. coli systems. On the education side, Prof. Malte Schwinger (educational psychology, Marburg) told them to use validated Likert-scale instruments instead of writing their own, and one evaluation expert advised against factual recall as the primary measure for the Teaching Toolbox.
good.realWorld: The team frames CLiPPR as enabling infrastructure for molecular farming rather than a product, and is candid that it is one of several missing pieces: chloroplast transformation is still not established in many plant species, selecting successful transformants is often as hard as making them, and the absence of post-translational processing limits which proteins can be made there. Fourteen molecular-farming stakeholders were interviewed on what integration would actually look like, covering compound classes, the advantages of stable transformants, inducer choice, production setup and regulation; Jess Bunchek and Dr. Don Stewart established that higher-plant molecular farming would realistically run in contained greenhouses rather than open fields. Containment is also a design argument, since in most higher plants the chloroplast is maternally inherited, so transgenes are not spread by pollen. Light-based induction via optogenetics was investigated with Lars Broker (PULSE system) because it costs nothing, leaves no residue, and is already applied by drone in modern agriculture, and is held as the most attractive long-term inducer from a safety standpoint. The five remaining application domains (agriculture, space, sustainability, law and regulation, scientific impact) each have their own analysis page, and the parts collection is the handover mechanism: documented, Registry-deposited, and intended for other teams doing organelle engineering and RNA-level regulation in plants.

images.caption: Screening the library of synthetic 5'UTR and designer PPR pairs in chloroplast cell-free extract, the lowest-complexity of the three test systems; one of these 30 de novo UTRs gave the highest transgene expression yet reported in a chloroplast in vitro.

Microscopy of PPR107 in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, confirming that a nuclear-encoded designer PPR is imported into the chloroplast, the step the whole 'outsource inducibility to the nucleus' design depends on.

Stacked plates for semi-automated protein purification in 96-well format: a fritted Ni-NTA plate, a filter plate and a flat-bottom plate assembled for centrifugation, adapted from the Baker Lab protocol for scaled characterisation of designed proteins.

Plasmid Panic, the team's escape game, redesigned after school visits showed students were far more curious about what daily lab life looks like than about the science content; released in English and German with multiple difficulty levels.

gemsTakeaway: Marburg's most transferable asset is the SciComm and Evaluation Guide mindset: decide the intended outcome first, use validated Likert instruments rather than home-made ones, and never accept attendance or enjoyment as evidence of learning ('reach is not impact, and satisfaction is not learning'). On the dry-lab side, copy their automation-as-design-decision argument: an acoustic liquid handler plus a planned plate layout does not just save pipetting, it shrinks reaction volumes fourfold, makes reagent budgets predictable in advance, and cuts variance, which is exactly what lets a small team characterise a real library instead of three constructs.
